passages.t: ‘Show me, O LORD, my end’: life as a breath
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. For Jeduthun. A Psalm of David” (verse 1). He had decided to keep quiet: “I will guard my mouth with a muzzle as long as the wicked are present” (verse 1). But silence did not help. “My heart grew hot within me; as I mused, the fire burned” (verse 3).

So he speaks, to God. “Show me, O LORD, my end and the measure of my days. Let me know how fleeting my life is” (verse 4). “You, indeed, have made my days as handbreadths” (verse 5). “Truly each man at his best exists as but a breath” (verse 5). People rush about and pile up money, “not knowing who will haul them away” (verse 6).

Then the turn: “And now, O Lord, for what do I wait? My hope is in You” (verse 7).

He asks for forgiveness and for relief from suffering. He calls himself “a foreigner dwelling with You, a stranger like all my fathers” (verse 12). And the psalm ends in an unusual, dark request: “Turn Your gaze away from me, that I may again be cheered before I depart and am no more” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Jeduthun was one of the leaders of music David appointed (1 Chronicles 16:41). His name also heads Psalms 62 and 77.

A handbreadth was the width of a hand, one of the smallest measures people used. A whole life, he says, is a few hands wide.

‘Breath’ in verse 5 is the Hebrew word hevel: a puff of air, vapour. It comes three times in this psalm (verses 5, 6 and 11). It is the same word that runs all through Ecclesiastes, where the BSB puts “Futility of futilities” (Ecclesiastes 1:2).

‘Foreigner’ and ‘stranger’ (verse 12) were people living in a land that was not theirs, with no land of their own, depending on the kindness of others. Israel's law told the people to protect them. He says that before God, every person is a guest.
passages.later:
James asks, “What is your life? You are a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes” (James 4:14). Jesus told of a rich man who piled up wealth and heard God say, “This very night your life will be required of you. Then who will own what you have accumulated?” (Luke 12:20), the very worry of verse 6.

Hebrews says the faithful of old “acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth” (Hebrews 11:13), and Peter calls Christians “foreigners and exiles” (1 Peter 2:11), using the language of verse 12.
passages.hard:
The psalm ends, ‘Turn Your gaze away from me.’ Is it right to ask God to leave you alone?

Job prayed something similar: “Leave me alone, for my days are but a breath” (Job 7:16). When pain feels like God's hand pressing down, a person may want only relief. The psalm does not pretend this is a good feeling. It records it honestly, and God kept it in the Bible. Like Psalm 88, this psalm ends before the light returns. Even so, verse 7 stands in the middle: ‘My hope is in You.’

If you feel that you want to ‘be no more’, please do not carry that alone. Speak to someone today, a pastor, a doctor, a trusted friend or a crisis line. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks:
The psalm asks you to count your days honestly. Not to frighten you, but to free you from rushing after things that will not last (verse 6).

And it asks where your hope is. When life is seen as a breath, verse 7 is the question that matters: ‘for what do I wait?’
